documents.title: EURETINA guidelines for management of retinal vein occlusion

chunks.content: Introduction Retinal vein occlusion (RVO) leads to visual loss second only to diabetic retinopathy. Its pathogenesis is mainly retinal vein stenosis or relaxation restriction, which, in turn, causes blood flow block or intravascular thrombosis. Retinal vein occlusion can be divided into central RVO (CRVO) and branch RVO (BRVO) [ ]. Worldwide, the prevalence of BRVO is approximately 0.4%, compared with 0.08% for CRVO, and is evenly distributed between men and women, with a higher risk in the elderly population [ ]. Macular oedema (MO), a leading cause of visual impairment, can occur with either CRVO or BRVO [ ]. The pathomechanism involves increased venous blood pressure and damage to the vessel wall, leading to fluid leakage [ ]. The accurate diagnosis and monitoring of RVO–MO have been revolutionised by advances in ocular imaging, particularly optical coherence tomography (OCT). Optical coherence tomography provides high-resolution, cross-sectional visualisation of retinal pathology, allowing clinicians to localise and delineate the extent of MO, detect associated features such as disorganisation of retinal inner layers (DRIL) or hyperreflective foci and objectively quantify central retinal thickness (CRT). These precise anatomical biomarkers are indispensable not only for diagnosis and treatment decisions with current therapies but also for defining the eligible patient population and treatment endpoints for emerging modalities, such as gene therapy [ – ]. Recently, research has focused on using anti-inflammatory and anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) therapeutic strategies to reduce MO and improve vision. Two established treatments are widely used in clinics: intravitreal ranibizumab (RNZ; Lucentis; Genentech, Inc., South San Francisco, CA, USA) and intravitreal dexamethasone (DEX; Ozurdex ® ; Allergan plc, Dublin, Ireland) implants, both of which have been approved for the treatment of RVO with MO in several countries [ ]. Dexamethasone sustained-release implants are coated with the Novadur ® solid polymer matrix (Allergan plc/AbbVie Inc.) containing the glucocorticoid DEX. The implant is injected into the vitreous cavity through the pars plana using a proprietary 22-gauge applicator. One study showed that DEX is present in the retina and vitreous for up to 6 months and reaches peak concentrations in the first 2 months after injection [ ]. Another study compared a 0.7-mg DEX vitreous implant, a 0.35-mg DEX implant and a sham injection for the treatment of MO secondary to BRVO and CRVO, revealing that DEX vitreous implants significantly reduced the risk of visual loss [ ]. In addition, a randomised controlled trial (RCT) of MO secondary to RVO found that a 0.7-mg DEX vitreous implant significantly improved visual acuity and anatomical outcomes in Chinese patients, and both best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) and CRT were better than sham injections within 3–4 months after a single DEX treatment [ ]. However, as a long-acting steroid preparation, DEX has some potential side effects, such as cataracts and glaucoma, which are more likely to occur at > 6 months of treatment and may require additional intraocular surgery, which can be regarded as a limitation of this treatment approach [ ]. At present, intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF, such as RNZ, bevacizumab and pegaptanib sodium, has become the main treatment for RVO complicated with MO [ , ]. However, due to its short half-life and short-acting effect, repeated injections are necessary after the effective concentration has been reduced. This not only increases the financial burden on patients but also introduces risks, such as infection and glaucoma, caused by intraocular injection [ ]. Based on the above research status, there are clearly many treatment methods for RVO complicated with MO. The most common treatment methods are intravitreal anti-VEGF drugs and intravitreal steroid drugs; however, it remains clinically challenging to determine which of these two treatment methods should be used [ ]. This is because the decision involves balancing their distinct profiles – anti-VEGF agents (e.g. RNZ) often provide rapid visual improvement but require frequent injections, whereas steroids (e.g. DEX implants) offer sustained therapy with fewer injections but carry a higher risk of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) and cataract progression [ – ]. Ranibizumab and DEX implants are two of the more commonly used anti-VEGF and intravitreal steroid drugs, and many separate clinical trials have confirmed their effectiveness. At present, only the results of single studies comparing the two therapeutic effects are available [ – ]. This study adopts a meta-analysis method to compare the efficacy of RNZ and DEX, providing evidence-based advice for the selection of clinical treatment methods. Therefore, this study collects the published literature and quantifies the clinical effect and safety of these two treatments systematically through a meta-analysis. Data and methods Literature search Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, the research team conducted a systematic search. The search cutoff date was 31 August 2025. During the search, subject headings and free words were combined for the queries. The search terms were as follows: (1) ‘retinal vein occlusion’ OR ‘retinal vein thrombosis’ OR ‘branch retinal vein occlusion’ OR ‘central retinal vein occlusion’; (2) ‘macular oedema’; (3) ‘intravitreal dexamethasone implant’ OR ‘dexamethasone’ OR ‘dexamethasone implant’ OR ‘Ozurdex’; and (4) ‘intravitreal ranibizumab’ OR ‘ranibizumab’ OR ‘Lucentis’. Inclusion and exclusion criteria The study type (RCT or retrospective study), participants (age and disease type), interventions (specific drugs and dosage range, such as 0.5 mg of RNZ) and outcome measures (measurement units and time points for BCVA, CRT, etc.) were further clarified. All included studies required quantitative data that could be used for meta-analysis. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) study type – RCT or retrospective; (2) study participants – adult patients with BRVO or CRVO complicated with MO (aged ≥ 18 years); (3) interventions – (i) RNZ group (intravitreal RNZ for patients with RVO complicated with MO) or (ii) DEX group (intravitreal DEX implants for patients with RVO complicated with MO); and (4) outcome measures – BCVA, CRT, IOP and number of injections. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) patients who had previously received intravitreal injection or laser therapy; (2) patients with complications introduced by other treatment methods; (3) incomplete data; (4) repeated published studies; and (5) reviews, case reports or other studies. Literature screening The literature screening and data extraction process was independently conducted by two researchers (LY and LYH). They were blinded to each other’s assessment results, meaning that they could not see each other’s decisions during the screening and evaluation process to reduce subjective bias. For consistency of the literature screening and data extraction, the inter-rater reliability, using the Kappa statistic for categorical variables (e.g. inclusion/exclusion decisions) and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for continuous variables (e.g. extracted means, standard deviations) were calculated. The final Kappa value was 0.85, and the ICC values were all > 0.9, indicating excellent consistency between the raters. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion and consultation with a third researcher (ZJ). Literature quality evaluation Two independent researchers assessed the risk. Risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane Handbook (version 5.1.0) [ ]. The literature quality was divided into three levels: Level A (completely meeting the criteria), Level B (partially meeting the criteria ) and Level C (not meeting the criteria). In case of disagreement, a third investigator was consulted to reach an agreement. For the quality evaluation of retrospective studies, the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS) [ ] was used, which is scored on three aspects: selection, comparability and exposure or outcome, with 1 point for each condition met and a total score of 9 points. Studies with scores < 5 were of low quality, and studies with scores ≥ 5 were of high quality. Statistical analysis In this study, the RevMan 5.3 statistical software package (The Cochrane Collaboration, London, UK) was used. For dichotomous data, odds ratios were used as effect measures; for continuous data, weighted mean differences (MDs) were used as effect measures, and effect sizes were presented as point estimates with their 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Heterogeneity among included studies was assessed through the heterogeneity test. The test level for meta-analysis was set at α = 0.05. Results Literature search results A total of 385 relevant articles were identified in the databases for this study. Following systematic screening, 10 eligible articles [ – ] were included for meta-analysis and systematic review (Fig. ). Basic characteristics A total of 1,274 patients with RVO complicated with MO treated with intravitreal RNZ or intravitreal DEX implants were included in 10 studies; there were 4 RCTs and 6 retrospective studies. The average age and gender of the patients in the literature were extracted, as well as the follow-up time (see Table ). The 4 RCTs included in this study were all evaluated using the risk assessment tool for bias in RCTs recommended in the Cochrane Handbook, and the quality rating of all the included literature was Level A (see Supplementary Table ). The NOS was used to evaluate the quality of the included retrospective studies, and the scores were 6–8. All the studies were of medium and high quality, which met the inclusion criteria (see Supplementary Table for details). Results of the meta-analysis Visual acuity changes Best-corrected visual acuity is an important functional index used to measure the effect of vision treatment. A meta-analysis of BCVA changes in patients with CRVO and BRVO complicated with MO was performed, making comparisons with the baseline at each follow-up point. Best-corrected visual acuity in central retinal vein occlusion The results of the pooled analysis of BCVA improvement in patients with CRVO for both treatment modalities are shown in Fig. . The results show that BCVA (based on Early Treatment of Diabetic Retinopathy Study [ETDRS] letters) improved more significantly in patients receiving intravitreal RNZ than in patients with CRVO receiving an intravitreal DEX implant (MD = 4.16, 95% CI: 0.44–7.88, p = 0.03). The subgroup analysis showed that the difference between groups was statistically significant ( p < 0.001), indicating that the follow-up time was the source of heterogeneity among BCVA indicators. Specifically, there was no obvious difference in BCVA improvement between the two treatment modalities at 1 and 12 months, and there was no heterogeneity between the studies at 1 month (MD = 0.93, 95% CI: −1.92 to 3.77, p = 0.52, I ² = 0.0%). At 6 months, however, BCVA improved more in the RNZ group than in the DEX group (MD = 9.51, 95% CI: 6.20–12.82, p < 0.001). Best-corrected visual acuity in branch retinal vein occlusion The results of the pooled analysis of BCVA improvement in patients with BRVO for both treatment modalities are shown in Fig. . The pooled analysis showed that, overall, there was no significant difference in BCVA improvement between the two treatment groups for BRVO (MD = − 0.04, 95% CI: −0.15 to 0.07, p = 0.49). Subgroup analysis by time points revealed a temporal pattern; RNZ provided superior BCVA improvement in the early phases, with a statistically significant advantage at 1 month (MD = 0.10, 95% CI: 0.04–0.15, p = 0.0004) and 3 months (MD = 0.06, 95% CI: 0.00–0.11, p = 0.03). At later time points (6 and 12 months), the point estimates of the MDs favoured the DEX implant; however, these results were not statistically significant (at 6 months: MD = − 0.15, 95% CI: −0.38 to 0.07, p = 0.18; at 12 months: MD = − 0.13, 95% CI: −0.76 to 0.50, p = 0.68). It is important to note that the results at 6 and 12 months were accompanied by considerable heterogeneity ( I ² = 70% and I ² = 97%, respectively). A subsequent sensitivity analysis by Ozkaya [ ] confirmed that RNZ significantly improved BCVA in patients with BRVO. Following exclusion, the heterogeneity decreased by 4%, and the heterogeneity between groups was statistically significant ( p = 0.003), indicating that the follow-up time was the source of heterogeneity in BCVA in BRVO (see Supplementary Fig. ). In this study, a meta-analysis was performed on the CRT changes in CRVO in patients with BRVO complicated with MO compared with baseline at each follow-up node. Patients with CRVO in the RNZ-treated group had a more significant reduction in CRT at 6 months (MD = − 158.83, 95% CI: −270.08 to − 47.57, p = 0.005), but there was high heterogeneity between studies ( I ² = 66.0%). The results showed that patients with BRVO treated with intravitreal RNZ had a significantly greater reduction in CRT than those treated with an intravitreal DEX implant (MD = − 41.25, 95% CI: −81.44 to − 1.05, p = 0.04). The subgroup analysis showed that the differences between groups were statistically significant ( p < 0.0001), indicating that the follow-up time was the source of heterogeneity in the CRT changes. Central retinal thickness decreased more significantly in the RNZ group than in the DEX group at 3 months (MD = − 92.10, 95% CI: −123.12 to − 61.08, p < 0.001) and 6 months (MD = − 67.01, 95% CI: −113.44 to − 20.59, p = 0.005). The substantial heterogeneity observed in this analysis may be attributed to several factors, including differences in study design (RCTs vs. retrospective studies), variations in the treatment protocols (e.g. fixed dosing vs. pro re nata regimens for RNZ) and diversity in patient baseline characteristics, such as the duration of MO and the extent of ischaemia, which were not consistently reported across all included studies. Despite this heterogeneity, the direction of effect consistently favoured RNZ at the 3- and 6-month time points in the subgroup analysis. Treatment-induced intraocular pressure changes in retinal vein occlusion Increased IOP is a common adverse reaction to the treatment of retinal diseases with intravitreal DEX implants and intravitreal RNZ. Figure shows the IOP changes observed with both treatments in this study. At 1 month after initiation of treatment, MD = − 2.98, 95% CI: −5.79 to − 0.17 and p = 0.04; the IOP in the DEX group increased at 3 months (MD = − 2.00, 95% CI: −2.51 to − 1.50, p < 0.001) and 6 months (MD = − 1.04, 95% CI: −2.02 to − 0.05, p = 0.04) and was higher than in the RNZ group. The pooled results of all included studies showed that the IOP increase in the DEX group was higher than that in the RNZ group after treatment (MD = − 1.82, 95% CI: −2.51 to − 1.12, p < 0.001). A sensitivity analysis by Kaldirim [ ] showed that DEX significantly influenced IOP changes resulting from treatment in patients with RVO. Following exclusion, the heterogeneity decreased by 2%, and the heterogeneity between groups was statistically significant ( p = 0.0007), indicating that the follow-up time was the source of heterogeneity (see Supplementary Fig. ). Number of injections used during the treatment of retinal vein occlusion The number of injections required for intravitreal DEX implants and intravitreal RNZ to treat RVO has been of concern to clinicians. This study analysed the number of injections after 6 and 12 months of RVO treatment included in the articles. The RNZ group received significantly more injections than the DEX group at 6 months (MD = 1.97, 95% CI: 1.38–2.55, p < 0.001) and 12 months (MD = 2.74, 95% CI: 2.31–3.17, p < 0.001) after treatment. The number of injections was higher in the RNZ group than in the DEX group (MD = 2.45, 95% CI: 1.97–2.94, p < 0.001) (see Fig. ). The heterogeneity between groups was statistically significant ( p = 0.04), indicating that the follow-up time was the source of heterogeneity. Publication bias Publication bias analysis was conducted on the above analysis indicators, and no obvious publication bias was found (see Supplementary Figs. – for details). Discussion Ten high-quality articles were included in this study, and the results were reliable. The meta-analysis demonstrated that intravitreal RNZ provided a greater improvement in BCVA and a more significant reduction in CRT than the DEX implant in patients with RVO complicated by MO. Furthermore, postoperative follow-up revealed a higher incidence of elevated IOP in the DEX group. The meta-analysis of this study showed that intravitreal RNZ was superior to intravitreal DEX implants in improving visual acuity in patients with BRVO and CRVO complicated by MO. Specifically, for patients with CRVO, BCVA (based on ETDRS letters) improved more significantly in RNZ-treated patients at 6 months ( p < 0.001). For patients with BRVO, RNZ treatment showed a greater BCVA improvement at 1 month ( p < 0.001) and 3 months ( p = 0.03). These results are consistent with those of previous studies. Specifically, for patients with CRVO, BCVA (based on ETDRS letters) improved more significantly in RNZ-treated patients at 6 months ( p < 0.001). For patients with BRVO, RNZ treatment showed a greater BCVA improvement at 1 month ( p < 0.001) and 3 months ( p = 0.03). These results are consistent with those of previous studies. For example, the BRAVO study assessed the efficacy and safety of intravitreal RNZ in patients with BRVO complicated by MO and found that 55% and 61% of patients treated with 0.3- and 0.5-mg doses of RNZ achieved a 3-line visual improvement, respectively, compared with only 29% in the control group [ , ]. Anatomically, RNZ was also more effective than the DEX implant in reducing CRT. Patients with BRVO exhibited significant CRT reductions at 3 and 6 months, whereas those with CRVO showed a pronounced effect at 6 months. This suggests that the potent anti-VEGF effect of RNZ leads to a rapid and substantial resolution of MO. The GENEVA study, which compared different DEX doses with sham surgery, supports the concept that the peak effect of steroids may not match the initial powerful anti-oedematous action of anti-VEGF agents [ ]. The observed efficacy of RNZ in our analysis at 6 months, for both BRVO and CRVO, highlights its potent short-to-medium-term activity. Elevated IOP is a well-documented adverse event of intravitreal corticosteroid therapy. Our results consistently showed that IOP was significantly higher in the DEX group than in the RNZ group at 3 and 6 months post-treatment. Clinically, this IOP elevation is often short-term and manageable with topical antihypertensive medications [ , ]. However, vigilant monitoring is essential, as a small subset of patients (e.g. 1.7% in the study by Capone et al. [ ]) may require surgical intervention for glaucoma. Consequently, the safety profile of RNZ regarding IOP is more favourable, although this must be balanced against its higher injection frequency. The injection quantity of intravitreal anti-VEGF drugs and intravitreal steroid drugs for the treatment of RVO has been an ongoing matter of concern; however, related studies have relatively few analyses of the impact of injection frequency on clinical efficacy. The results of the meta-analysis of this study showed that at 6 and 12 months after the start of treatment, the number of injections in the RNZ group was significantly higher than that in the DEX group. The study by Yoon et al. [ ] evaluated the treatment of patients with RVO combined with MO using intravitreal DEX implants. During the 12-month period, 32% and 49% of the patients received one and three injections, respectively. Patients requiring three injections had a higher CRT and larger macular non-perfusion at baseline. In addition, adverse events, such as increased IOP (35%) and newly diagnosed cataracts (16%), occurred. The increased injection frequency of intravitreal RNZ may impose an economic burden and an increased risk of adverse reactions on patients. However, due to the different basic conditions of patients, the choice of treatment methods still needs to be determined based on the patients’ situations. For patients with RVO–MO who already have a high IOP or glaucoma factors, the advantages and disadvantages of the two treatments should be explained to them, and intravitreal RNZ treatment can be recommended. For patients with some economic pressure and no risk factors for glaucoma or cataracts, the advantage of an intravitreal DEX implant lies in the slow and stable release of the drug after a single injection, reducing the safety hazards and economic burden associated with frequent injections. In addition, the DEX implant has been included in the medical insurance reimbursement list for RVO–MO treatment since 2020 in China; therefore, it is a better choice for such patients [ , ]. Our findings can be contextualised by comparing them with the earlier systematic review and meta-analysis by Hu et al. [ ], which also compared intravitreal DEX implants and anti-VEGF agents for the treatment of RVO-related MO. This study, which included 5 RCTs with 873 patients published up to August 2018, concluded that there were no significant differences in BCVA and CRT between the two treatment groups at the primary endpoint, although it noted a substantial reduction in CRT favouring anti-VEGF agents in a subset of studies at 6 months [ ]. First, we incorporated a more recent and extensive body of literature, including 10 studies (4 RCTs and 6 retrospective studies) with a total of 1,274 patients, almost doubling the sample size and enhancing the statistical power and generalisability of the conclusions. First, we incorporated a more recent and extensive body of literature, including 10 studies (4 RCTs and 6 retrospective studies) with a total of 1,274 patients, almost doubling the sample size and enhancing the statistical power and generalisability of the conclusions. Second, although Hu et al. [ ] combined different types of RVO (CRVO and BRVO) and different anti-VEGF agents, our study performed detailed subgroup analyses based on the type of occlusion (CRVO vs. BRVO) and specific time points (1, 3, 6 and 12 months), providing a more nuanced and clinically relevant understanding of the differential treatment effects over time. For example, we were able to demonstrate that RNZ was superior to DEX in improving BCVA at 6 months for CRVO and at 1 and 3 months for BRVO and in reducing CRT at 3 and 6 months for both types, findings that were not fully elucidated in the previous meta-analysis. Furthermore, our analysis provided a more comprehensive and quantitative assessment of safety outcomes. We confirmed that the DEX implant was associated with a significantly higher risk of IOP elevation, a finding consistent with that of Hu et al. [ ]. However, we also extended the safety profile comparison by quantitatively analysing the number of injections required, clearly showing that the RNZ group received considerably more injections over 6 and 12 months, which is a crucial factor for treatment burden and healthcare economics. Finally, the inclusion of non-RCT evidence (retrospective studies) in our review, although a limitation in terms of design hierarchy, allows for the incorporation of ‘real-world’ effectiveness data and longer-term outcomes, offering a complementary perspective to that of the rigorous but sometimes restrictive environment of RCTs. In summary, although the core conclusion of Hu et al. [ ] – that both modalities are effective – remains valid, our updated and more extensive analysis provides a finer-grained, temporally resolved and clinically differentiated comparison that can better inform personalised treatment decisions for patients with RVO-related MO. This study has several limitations. The results of the meta-analysis were obtained from different types of research designs, which may have led to bias. Second, a key limitation of our analysis is that most included studies did not stratify outcomes based on the ischaemic subtype of the RVO. Ischaemic status is a known prognostic factor, and the treatment response may differ between ischaemic and non-ischaemic variants. Consequently, our results represent an average effect across these subtypes. Future studies designed to compare RNZ and DEX implants should aim to provide subgroup analyses based on ischaemia to guide more personalised treatment approaches. Third, the potential influence of specific baseline clinical and OCT biomarkers on treatment response could not be assessed in this meta-analysis. Parameters such as lens status (e.g. pseudophakia) or the presence of specific OCT features, such as subretinal fluid (SRF) or DRIL, may predispose patients to a differential response to anti-VEGF therapy versus steroids. For example, patients with pseudophakia may be better candidates for steroid implants due to the eliminated risk of cataract progression. Similarly, the presence of SRF has been suggested in some studies to be associated with a more favourable response to anti-VEGF agents. However, the included studies did not provide stratified outcomes based on these parameters. Therefore, our results represent an average effect across heterogeneous patient profiles. Future studies should aim to analyse whether such biomarkers can serve as predictors for selecting the most effective initial therapy (anti-VEGF or steroid) on an individualised basis. Furthermore, due to the limitation of the follow-up time, the long-term therapeutic effects of the two treatment methods for > 1 year cannot be evaluated. Therefore, it is necessary to incorporate more high-quality, large-sample and long-term follow-up studies in the future to further confirm the value of the results established by the meta-analysis. This would assist in the rational selection of the treatment timing of intravitreal RNZ and intravitreal DEX implants in clinical practice. Although the current standard of care for RVO–MO revolves around repeated anti-VEGF injections or sustained-release steroids, the ultimate therapeutic goal remains achieving durable efficacy with a minimal treatment burden. By directly comparing the two predominant treatment modalities, this meta-analysis provides a robust clinical context for evaluating emerging therapies, notably gene therapy. By directly comparing the two predominant treatment modalities, this meta-analysis provides a robust clinical context for evaluating emerging therapies, notably gene therapy. The findings of this study underscore a fundamental clinical challenge: the trade-off between efficacy and treatment frequency. Ranibizumab, although effective, requires frequent intravitreal injections to maintain its benefits, which poses a considerable burden on patients, caregivers and healthcare systems. Gene therapy approaches for retinal diseases aim to address this limitation by enabling the sustained endogenous production of anti-angiogenic proteins (e.g. anti-VEGF agents) from a single administration. The efficacy profile of RNZ established in this analysis helps to define the therapeutic benchmark that these novel gene-based treatments must meet or exceed. Furthermore, the sustained anti-inflammatory and anti-oedematous effect observed with the DEX implant, albeit with a different safety profile, provides proof of concept that long-acting therapies are viable and desirable for managing a chronic condition such as RVO–MO. This supports the development rationale for gene therapies designed for sustained expression. Therefore, the results of this meta-analysis not only inform current clinical choices between RNZ and DEX but also contribute valuable comparative data that can guide the design and evaluation of future gene therapy trials, potentially changing the long-term standard of care from chronic reinjection to a one-time treatment. Furthermore, the evolution towards targeted and personalised therapies underscores the critical importance of precise diagnostic biomarkers. The research by Iglicki et al. and other scholars has been instrumental in identifying and validating OCT-based biomarkers (e.g. DRIL and ORYD) that predict treatment response and disease progression in retinal diseases [ , , , ]. The application of these precise imaging criteria for patient selection was a foundational element in the studies we analysed. This approach ensures that the clinical outcomes compared in this meta-analysis are based on a well-defined pathological substrate. For future gene therapy trials, which require meticulous patient stratification and long-term monitoring, the reliance on such objective, quantifiable ancillary tests will be paramount to demonstrate efficacy and ensure that treatment is delivered to those with the precise pathology it aims to address. The findings of this meta-analysis hold substantial practical implications for ophthalmologists worldwide. First, this study provides a synthesised, evidence-based comparison of two fundamental treatment paradigms for RVO–MO: the potent but short-acting anti-VEGF strategy (RNZ) and the sustained-release anti-inflammatory strategy (DEX implant). For ophthalmologists in diverse healthcare settings – from high-volume centres in developed countries to resource-limited environments – this analysis offers critical insights to tailor treatment choices. The superior early visual gains with RNZ may be preferred in settings where frequent monitoring and injection are feasible. Conversely, the sustained efficacy and reduced injection frequency of the DEX implant present a valuable option for patients with limited access to frequent healthcare or those struggling with treatment adherence. This evidence is crucial for optimising individual patient care and for guiding the development of efficient, context-aware treatment protocols on a global scale. Second, by rigorously quantifying the distinct efficacy and safety profiles of each drug over time, this analysis empowers clinicians to make informed decisions and set realistic patient expectations. Understanding that RNZ may offer faster initial results, whereas DEX provides longer-lasting effects with fewer injections but a higher risk of elevated IOP, is essential for shared decision-making. Furthermore, the comprehensive safety comparison alerts clinicians to the necessary postoperative monitoring strategies for each treatment. For readers, this study delivers directly applicable evidence. It moves beyond the results of single trials to provide a consolidated, higher-level conclusion that can be immediately integrated into clinical reasoning. It addresses a common and challenging clinical dilemma with a clear, data-driven narrative, thereby fulfilling the journal’s mission to publish content that has a direct and positive impact on ophthalmic care worldwide. Conclusion Taking the current study evidence together with the results of this meta-analysis, we conclude that intravitreal RNZ is superior to DEX implants in improving BCVA and reducing CRT in patients with RVO complicated by MO. Specifically, RNZ was more effective in improving BCVA and reducing CRT in the early stages of BRVO, whereas it took longer to show efficacy in patients with CRVO. It is important to note that the long-term comparative efficacy (beyond 12 months) of intravitreal RNZ versus the DEX implant remains less defined due to the limited follow-up duration of the included studies. Future large-scale RCTs with longer follow-up periods are warranted to confirm the sustainability of these therapeutic effects and to establish optimal long-term treatment strategies for RVO-associated MO. However, both treatments have their advantages and disadvantages. For patients with RVO combined with MO treated with intravitreal RNZ, the injection frequency was higher than that of the DEX group, and the duration of therapeutic effect was shorter. Moreover, some of the literature indicates that its improvement in deep vascular complex blood flow is limited [ ]. By contrast, the intravitreal DEX implant requires fewer injections than intravitreal RNZ, has a longer duration of therapeutic effect [ ] and helps reduce the levels of inflammatory factors [ ]. However, it has disadvantages, such as a relatively high risk of elevated IOP, a high risk of secondary glaucoma and a slow onset, which require close attention during the clinical treatment process. For patients with RVO–MO who already have a high IOP or glaucoma factors, intravitreal RNZ treatment can be recommended. For patients with some economic pressure and no risk factors for glaucoma or cataracts, the intravitreal DEX implant reduces safety hazards and the economic burden. Therefore, in clinical practice, exploring the possibility of combined medication and providing targeted medication based on the individual conditions of patients should be the direction for future clinical research. documents.title: EURETINA guidelines for management of diabetic macular edema

chunks.content: Introduction and background Diabetic macular edema (DME) is a leading cause of vision impairment in patients with diabetic retinopathy, affecting approximately 7.6% of individuals with diabetes worldwide [ ]. This condition arises from chronic hyperglycemia-induced damage to retinal blood vessels, leading to increased vascular permeability, fluid accumulation in the macula (the central portion of the retina responsible for sharp, detailed vision), and consequent retinal thickening [ ]. If left untreated, DME can result in progressive and often irreversible vision loss, significantly impacting quality of life and functional independence. The pathophysiology of DME centers on the overproduction of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), a signaling protein that promotes pathological angiogenesis (abnormal blood vessel growth) and vascular leakage [ ]. This understanding led to the development of anti-VEGF agents, medications administered by intravitreal injection (directly into the vitreous cavity of the eye) that block VEGF activity, thereby reducing retinal swelling and preserving or improving vision. These agents have revolutionized DME treatment over the past two decades, replacing earlier approaches such as laser photocoagulation, which primarily aimed to prevent further vision loss rather than restore lost vision. Several anti-VEGF agents are currently available for the management of DME. Ranibizumab (Lucentis®) and aflibercept (Eylea®) are FDA-approved fragment and fusion protein formulations, respectively, specifically designed for intraocular use. Bevacizumab (Avastin®), originally developed for colorectal cancer, is widely used off-label as a cost-effective alternative. More recently, next-generation agents have entered clinical practice: brolucizumab (Beovu®), a single-chain antibody fragment with high VEGF-binding affinity, and faricimab (Vabysmo®), the first bispecific antibody designed for intraocular use that simultaneously inhibits both VEGF-A and angiopoietin-2 (Ang-2), a second pathway implicated in vascular instability and inflammation [ ]. Treatment outcomes in DME are typically assessed using two key measurements: best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), quantified as the number of letters read on a standardized Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) eye chart (with higher scores indicating better vision), and central retinal thickness (CRT), measured in micrometers (µm) using optical coherence tomography (OCT), a non-invasive imaging technique that provides cross-sectional images of the retina. Reductions in CRT indicate resolution of macular swelling, while gains in BCVA letters reflect functional visual improvement. The landmark DRCR.net Protocol T study provided pivotal comparative effectiveness data, demonstrating that aflibercept achieved superior gains in visual acuity (VA) among patients with baseline vision of 20/50 or worse. In contrast, all three agents (ranibizumab, aflibercept, and bevacizumab) showed comparable effects in milder cases [ , ]. Despite these advances, significant uncertainties persist. The real-world studies consistently report lower visual gains than those reported in RCTs, attributable to factors such as treatment non-adherence, delayed initiation, and variable patient comorbidities, including glycemic control and baseline CRT [ ]. This meta-analysis aimed to consolidate existing evidence on the efficacy and safety of anti-VEGF agents in DME, addressing gaps in comparative effectiveness and long-term outcomes. By synthesizing data from RCTs and observational studies, this study would provide comparative efficacy and safety data on anti-VEGF agents for treating DME, with a primary endpoint of the mean change in BCVA in ETDRS letters at 12 months. Review Methodology This meta-analysis followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines to systematically identify, evaluate, and synthesize studies on anti-VEGF agents in DME. A comprehensive search was conducted across several databases from 2010 to December 2024. Eligible studies included RCTs and prospective cohort studies comparing anti-VEGF agents (ranibizumab, aflibercept, and bevacizumab) with sham injections or other treatments. Search Strategy Description The following electronic databases were searched from January 1, 2010, to December 31, 2024: PubMed (MEDLINE), Embase (Ovid), Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Web of Science, and Scopus. The final search was performed on December 15, 2024. Reference lists of all included studies and relevant systematic reviews were hand-searched to identify additional eligible articles. No language restrictions were applied during the initial search, though non-English articles were subsequently assessed for eligibility using translation services where necessary (Table ). Additional studies were identified through hand-searching the reference lists of included articles and relevant reviews. Two reviewers independently screened titles/abstracts, with discrepancies resolved by a third reviewer. Cohen’s kappa (κ > 0.80) ensured high inter-rater agreement. PICO - Based Study Selection Process The PICO framework ensured only high-quality studies were included. RCTs and cohort studies with ≥6 months follow-up were prioritized. Studies lacking comparative outcomes or with high attrition bias were excluded (Table ). Protocol for Data Extraction Two reviewers independently extracted data using a predefined Excel template that included study characteristics (author, year), patient demographics, treatment regimen, and outcomes. Discrepancies were resolved via consensus. To ensure consistency across studies, outcome data were extracted at standardized time points. The primary efficacy outcome, mean change in BCVA from baseline, was extracted at 12 months (±3 months) when available. For studies reporting outcomes at multiple follow-up durations, the

only high-quality studies were included. RCTs and cohort studies with ≥6 months follow-up were prioritized. Studies lacking comparative outcomes or with high attrition bias were excluded (Table ). Protocol for Data Extraction Two reviewers independently extracted data using a predefined Excel template that included study characteristics (author, year), patient demographics, treatment regimen, and outcomes. Discrepancies were resolved via consensus. To ensure consistency across studies, outcome data were extracted at standardized time points. The primary efficacy outcome, mean change in BCVA from baseline, was extracted at 12 months (±3 months) when available. For studies reporting outcomes at multiple follow-up durations, the following hierarchy was applied: 12-month data were prioritized as the primary endpoint, followed by 24-month data for long-term efficacy assessment, and, when longer follow-up was unavailable, six-month data. CRT measurements were extracted at the corresponding time points. For studies reporting outcomes exclusively at non-standard intervals (e.g., 9 months or 18 months), the nearest available time point to 12 months was selected, and this deviation was recorded for sensitivity analysis. In studies that reported outcomes at multiple time points within the same publication (e.g., 6, 12, and 24 months), all time points were extracted to enable longitudinal assessment. Still, only the 12-month data were used in the primary meta-analysis to maintain temporal consistency across studies. Quality and Bias Assessment of the Studies ROB 2.0 (Cochrane Collaboration, Bristol, UK) assessed randomization, blinding, and selective reporting in RCTs [ ], while ROBINS-E (Cochrane Collaboration, Bristol, UK) evaluated confounding in observational studies [ ]. Funnel plots and Egger’s test (p < 0.05) detected publication bias [ ]. Statistical Approach A random-effects model (DerSimonian-Laird) pooled mean differences (MD) for BCVA/CRT and risk ratios (RR) for AEs. I² > 50% indicated significant heterogeneity. Subgroup analyses explored differences by anti-VEGF type and baseline severity. Sensitivity analyses excluded high-bias studies. Results Study Selection for Systematic Review The systematic review process began with the identification of 2,632 records from five databases: PubMed (n = 953), Embase (n = 569), Web of Science (n = 576), Cochrane Library (n = 250), and Scopus (n = 279). After removing 1,573 duplicate records, 1,059 studies underwent title/abstract screening, resulting in 983 exclusions due to irrelevance. Full-text retrieval was attempted for 76 reports; 45 were unavailable, leaving 31 studies for eligibility assessment. Ultimately, 10 studies were excluded due to unmet PICO criteria (e.g., incorrect population, intervention, or outcomes) (Table ) [ - ], while 21 studies met the inclusion criteria (Figure ) [ , - ]. Aflibercept and faricimab showed superior outcomes in severe DME, with extended dosing intervals (e.g., faricimab every 16 weeks). Bevacizumab and biosimilars are cost-effective but might require more frequent injections. Brolucizumab has a higher risk. Faricimab and AI-based predictive models (e.g., GAN) represent advancements in personalized treatment (Table ). The meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy and safety of anti-VEGF agents (aflibercept, bevacizumab, ranibizumab, faricimab, and brolucizumab) in DME. Key findings from the included studies include efficacy and safety outcomes, baseline severity, and treatment regimens. As per the findings of the included studies, aflibercept demonstrated superior VA gains (+8-10 letters) and greater reductions in CRT compared to bevacizumab and ranibizumab, particularly in patients with baseline VA ≤20/50 [ , ]. This superiority was particularly evident in the Protocol T trials, where aflibercept-treated patients achieved three to five additional letters of VA improvement compared with those receiving bevacizumab at a two-year follow-up [ ]. Faricimab, as reported in the included studies, was non-inferior to ranibizumab with extended dosing intervals (every 16 weeks), thereby reducing treatment burden [ , ]. The YOSEMITE and RHINE trials confirmed that faricimab maintained VA improvements (+10.1 letters at 2 years) with fewer injections, significantly reducing treatment burden [ ]. Furthermore, bevacizumab, while cost-effective, required more frequent injections (every four to six weeks) to achieve comparable improvements in VA and CRT, as reported by Hutton et al. [ ]. Biosimilars of bevacizumab demonstrated efficacy similar to that of the reference product, making them a viable, low-cost alternative [ ]. Safety profiles, as synthesized from the included studies, varied across anti-VEGF agents. For instance, the meta-analysis by Abu Serhan et al. [ ] reported that brolucizumab was associated with a higher risk of intraocular inflammation and retinal vasculitis compared to other agents. Bevacizumab and biosimilars had no new safety signals, with low rates of systemic AEs such as stroke and myocardial infarction [ ]. Aflibercept and ranibizumab exhibited similar safety profiles, with rare cases of endophthalmitis (<1%) and retinal detachment (0.5%) [ ]. Long-term studies (5+ years) confirmed durable efficacy but revealed persistent macular thickening in 20-30% of patients, suggesting treatment resistance in some cases [ ]. Long-term studies (5+ years) confirmed durable efficacy but revealed persistent macular thickening in 20-30% of patients, suggesting treatment resistance in some cases [ ]. Risk of Bias Assessment for Included Studies Risk of bias: ROB-2 was applied to 12 RCTs, revealing low risk of bias in randomization (D1), adherence to protocols (D2), and outcome measurement (D4), supporting the reliability of these trials. Similarly, the ROBINS-E assessment of nine non-randomized studies demonstrated low risk of bias across all domains, including confounding (D1), exposure measurement (D2), and outcome reporting (D7), indicating robust methodological quality. Both assessments highlighted the high internal validity of the included studies, with no significant methodological flaws detected in either randomized or non-randomized designs. The consistent low-risk ratings support the strength of evidence for meta-analytic conclusions regarding anti-VEGF therapies in DME (Figures - ). Publication bias: The funnel plot (Figure ) displays the distribution of effect sizes (ranging from -10.00 to +15.00 ETDRS letters) against their standard errors (0.40 to 1.60) for studies evaluating anti-VEGF agents in DME. Visual inspection of the plot reveals minimal publication bias, as asymmetry would typically manifest as an absence of studies in regions corresponding to negative or null findings with large standard errors (typically small studies). The trim-and-fill method imputed hypothetical missing studies to assess the potential impact of unpublished negative findings, and the adjusted pooled estimate remained consistent with the observed estimate, further supporting the absence of substantial publication bias. Egger's regression test was used to assess funnel plot asymmetry quantitatively (Table ). The intercept (bias) was 5.99 (95% CI: 4.57 to 7.42) with a standard error of 0.68. The t-value of 8.78 and associated p-value of <0.001 indicate statistically significant asymmetry. The slope (0.81, 95% CI: 0.72 to 0.90) represents the estimated treatment effect, independent of small-study effects, and confirms the consistent positive benefit of anti-VEGF therapy across studies [ , ]. Meta - Analysis Findings Forest plot: The forest plot synthesizes data from 21 studies evaluating the efficacy of various anti-VEGF agents in DME, measured by VA improvement (ETDRS letters). The effect sizes range from 0.85 [ ] to 10.30 letters [ ], with most estimates clustered between 3.70 and 8.20 letters. The diamond-shaped markers represent point estimates, while horizontal lines show 95% confidence intervals; notably, all studies demonstrate statistically significant benefits, as their CIs exclude zero. Weighting percentages (1.57-12.06%) reflect each study's contribution to the pooled analysis, with larger weights given to more precise estimates (12.03%) [ ]. The substantial variation in effect magnitudes likely reflects differences in baseline severity, specific anti-VEGF agents used, and treatment protocols. The consistent rightward positioning of all effects confirms the overall therapeutic benefit of anti-VEGF therapy for DME across diverse clinical contexts and study designs (Figure ). Heterogeneity assessment: The random-effects meta-analysis of 21 studies demonstrated a statistically significant overall MD of 2.96 ETDRS letters (95% CI: 1.75 to 4.16, p < 0.001) favoring anti-VEGF therapy over comparators for improvement in VA in DME. However, this pooled estimate must be interpreted with substantial caution due to substantial heterogeneity (I² = 97.19%, τ² = 0.19, Cochran's Q = 712.77, p < 0.001). This exceptionally high I² value indicates that approximately 97% of the observed variance across studies is attributable to true differences in effect sizes rather than random sampling error, leaving only 3% of the variability explained by chance. The wide prediction interval (1.45 to 4.46 letters) further underscores this heterogeneity, suggesting that while the true treatment effect in future clinical settings is expected to be positive, its magnitude may range from modest (approximately 1.5 letters) to clinically meaningful (approximately 4.5 letters) depending on specific patient populations, treatment protocols, and contextual factors. The substantial heterogeneity observed is not unexpected given the diversity of included studies across several key dimensions: different anti-VEGF agents with varying mechanisms of action and binding affinities (aflibercept, ranibizumab, bevacizumab, faricimab, brolucizumab); variable baseline disease severity (mild to severe DME); differing dosing regimens (monthly, extended interval, PRN); heterogeneous follow-up durations (six months to five years); and inclusion of both clinical trial and real-world data. While subgroup analyses by drug class, baseline severity, and dosing regimen were performed to explore sources of heterogeneity, the persistently high within-subgroup I² values (>96%) indicate that these factors alone do not fully account for the observed variability. This suggests that additional patient-level factors, including glycemic control (HbA1c), duration of diabetes, prior treatment exposure, baseline CRT, and specific morphological features on OCT, likely contribute importantly to heterogeneity in treatment response. Future research should prioritize individual-patient data meta-analyses to characterize these effect modifiers

Future research should prioritize individual-patient data meta-analyses to characterize these effect modifiers better and enable more precise treatment matching (Table ) [ ]. Subgroup analysis: The stratified analysis by drug class revealed important differential efficacy among anti-VEGF agents, with aflibercept (7.02 letters, 95% CI: 4.42-9.61) and faricimab/brolucizumab (6.45 letters) showing the strongest point estimates for VA improvement, while bevacizumab (3.03 letters) and ranibizumab (3.38 letters) demonstrated more modest benefits. However, these findings must be interpreted with appropriate caution due to substantial statistical heterogeneity that persists even after stratification. The within-subgroup heterogeneity remained exceptionally high (I² > 96% for all drug classes), indicating that the classification by drug alone does not fully account for the variability in treatment outcomes across studies. Furthermore, the pseudo R² value of 25.75% quantitatively confirms that drug class explains only approximately one-quarter of the total variance in treatment effects, leaving a substantial majority (approximately 75%) of variability attributable to other unmeasured or unaccounted factors, such as differences in baseline patient characteristics, treatment protocols, follow-up duration, or study design. These observations suggest that while drug class is a meaningful determinant of treatment response, it represents only one component of a complex, multifactorial landscape influencing outcomes in DME. The wide prediction intervals observed across subgroups further emphasize that individual patient responses may vary considerably despite class-level patterns. Therefore, these subgroup findings should be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive. They support the concept of personalized treatment selection based on drug class characteristics while underscoring the critical need for future research to identify and incorporate additional moderators of treatment efficacy, including glycemic control, retinal perfusion status, genetic factors, and specific morphological features on OCT, into predictive models that can guide more precise, individualized therapeutic decisions (Figure , Table ). This analysis presented a stratified meta-analysis of anti-VEGF treatment efficacy based on baseline DME severity, categorizing studies into three groups: Group A (severe DME, VA ≤20/50), Group B (mild-moderate DME, VA >20/50), and Group C (other/unspecified). The analysis revealed differential treatment responses across severity subgroups, with the most pronounced effects observed in severe DME cases (Group A), demonstrating effect sizes ranging from 6.80 to 8.20 ETDRS letters. Mild-moderate DME cases (Group B) showed more modest improvements (1.80-4.50 letters), while the heterogeneous Group C exhibited variable outcomes (0.85-10.30 letters). The combined effect size (2.61-4.10 letters) with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 97.19%) underscores the importance of baseline VA in predicting treatment response. Notably, studies in severe DME consistently occupied the higher end of the effect size spectrum, suggesting that patients with worse baseline vision may derive greater absolute benefit from anti-VEGF therapy. The wide prediction intervals (0.28-6.96) highlighted significant variability in individual treatment responses within each severity category, emphasizing the need for personalized treatment approaches considering baseline disease characteristics (Figure ). This stratified meta-analysis evaluated anti-VEGF efficacy across different treatment regimens, revealing significant variability in outcomes based on dosing frequency. Monthly dosing (Group A) demonstrated the most robust and consistent treatment effects (8.27 letters, 95% CI: 6.27-10.26), with minimal heterogeneity (I² = 0%), suggesting reliable performance across studies. Extended interval regimens (8-16 weeks, Group B) showed comparable peak efficacy (7.98 letters) but with substantially wider confidence intervals (-1.40 to 17.36) and high heterogeneity (I² = 93.95%), indicating variable success in maintaining treatment effects with less frequent dosing. PRN (Group C) and bimonthly/quarterly regimens (Group D) exhibited more modest effects (5.30 and 2.22 letters, respectively) with similarly wide prediction intervals, reflecting challenges in maintaining consistent visual gains with flexible dosing. The combined effect size (5.04 letters, 95% CI: 2.20-7.88) masks this important variability, as evidenced by the extremely wide prediction interval (-2.99 to 13.07) and high overall heterogeneity (I² = 97.19%). These findings suggested that while extended dosing intervals might achieve comparable efficacy in some patients, monthly regimens currently offer the most predictable outcomes, with PRN and less frequent dosing strategies requiring careful patient selection and monitoring. The substantial residual heterogeneity within each dosing subgroup underscores the need for personalized treatment approaches considering individual patient characteristics and treatment response patterns (Figure ). Discussion This meta-analysis provided comprehensive evidence supporting the efficacy and safety of anti-VEGF agents in DME, while revealing important differences in treatment outcomes across drug classes, dosing regimens, and baseline disease severity. The findings of the current analysis offer several clinically significant insights that both confirm and extend the current understanding of DME management. The demonstrated superiority of aflibercept in severe DME (VA ≤20/50) represented a key finding that aligns with and strengthens evidence from the landmark DRCR.net Protocol T trials. These trials first established that patients treated with aflibercept achieved a three- to five-letter gain in VA compared with bevacizumab at a two-year follow-up [ ]. The current analysis not only confirms this pattern across a broader range of studies but also provides quantitative estimates of the magnitude of benefit (8.2 letters for aflibercept vs. 3.7 letters for bevacizumab in severe cases). This differential efficacy might be explained by aflibercept's higher VEGF-binding affinity and broader target profile, which appear particularly advantageous in cases with more advanced disease. The emergence of faricimab as an effective option with extended dosing intervals represented an important advancement in DME treatment paradigms. The current study findings regarding faricimab's non-inferiority to ranibizumab with dosing every 16 weeks corroborate results from the pivotal YOSEMITE/RHINE trials [ ]. This extended dosing potential, coupled with faricimab's novel mechanism of dual Ang-2/VEGF-A inhibition, addresses two critical unmet needs in DME management: reducing treatment burden and targeting multiple pathological pathways. The durability of faricimab's treatment effect (maintaining +10.1 letters at two years) suggests it may offer particular advantages for patients with compliance challenges or limited access to frequent clinic visits. The cost-effectiveness of bevacizumab, despite its higher injection frequency, remains an important consideration for healthcare systems worldwide. The current study's results support real-world data [ ], which show that while bevacizumab requires more frequent administration to achieve comparable outcomes, it remains a valuable option in resource-constrained settings. The similar efficacy of bevacizumab biosimilars to the reference product, as demonstrated in the current analysis, further enhances access to affordable treatment options. The substantial heterogeneity observed (I² = 97.19%) presented both a challenge and an opportunity for deeper understanding. This variability, consistent with previous meta-analyses [ ], likely stems from multiple factors, including differences in study protocols, patient populations, treatment durations, and outcome measurement techniques. Notably, the current study's subgroup analyses revealed that monthly dosing schedules yielded the most consistent visual outcomes, whereas PRN regimens showed greater variability in treatment effects. The real-world outcomes reported by Mehta et al. [ ], synthesizing data from over 40,000 eyes across multiple international registries, including the Fight Retinal Blindness! Registry and European cohorts confirm that VA gains in routine clinical practice are generally lower than those achieved in tightly controlled randomized trials, highlighting the importance of treatment adherence and regular monitoring to optimize long-term outcomes. Safety findings from the current study analysis provide important guidance for clinical decision-making. The elevated risk of intraocular inflammation with brolucizumab [ ] contrasts with the favorable safety profiles of other agents, particularly regarding systemic adverse events. The low systemic risks associated with bevacizumab biosimilars [ ] reinforce their position as a safe option for patients with cardiovascular concerns. The current study's stratified analysis by baseline disease severity offers novel insights into treatment personalization. The greater absolute VA gains observed in severe DME (6.80-8.20 letters) than in mild-moderate cases support treatment escalation based on disease severity, consistent with EURETINA guidelines [ ]. This finding has important implications for clinical practice, suggesting that more potent agents such as aflibercept may be preferred for patients with worse baseline vision. The finding that drug class explained only 25.75% of the observed variance in treatment outcomes highlighted the multifactorial nature of DME treatment response. This underscores the need for future research to explore additional moderators of treatment efficacy, including glycemic control, retinal perfusion status, genetic factors, and specific morphological features on OCT. Such investigations could lead to more precise, personalized treatment approaches that optimize outcomes for individual patients. The implications of these findings for clinical practice are substantial. The current study results supported a stratified treatment approach in which aflibercept is prioritized for severe DME cases, faricimab is considered for patients who might benefit from extended dosing intervals, bevacizumab remains a cost-effective option when resources are limited, and brolucizumab is used cautiously due to safety concerns. These recommendations align with evolving treatment paradigms that emphasize both efficacy and practical considerations, such as treatment burden and cost-effectiveness. Limitations

Limitations of the study Several limitations of this meta-analysis must be acknowledged when interpreting the findings. First, the high statistical heterogeneity observed across analyses (I² > 95% in pooled estimates and >96% in most subgroup analyses) indicates substantial variability in treatment effects that is not fully explained by drug class, baseline severity, or dosing regimen, with the pseudo R² value of 25.75% confirming that drug class alone explains only one-quarter of the variance in outcomes and leaving approximately 75% attributable to unmeasured factors such as differences in study populations, glycemic control, duration of follow-up, prior treatment exposure, and OCT morphological features. Second, the geographic concentration of included studies in North America, Europe, and Japan limits generalizability to underrepresented populations, including India, the Middle East, Africa, and Southeast Asia, where differences in genetic background, healthcare infrastructure, and disease presentation may influence outcomes. Third, the safety analysis primarily focuses on ocular adverse events, with limited depth on systemic thromboembolic risk and cardiovascular outcomes, as most included studies were not powered to detect differences in these rare events. Fourth, regarding citation appropriateness, the excluded studies listed in Table , including those focused on liver cancer, oncology, and AMD, were identified during the initial broad search but correctly excluded from the final synthesis, serving only to document the screening process transparently in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Fifth, real-world data remain underrepresented relative to RCTs, potentially leading to overestimation of efficacy compared with routine clinical practice, where treatment adherence and comorbidity management are often suboptimal. Finally, safety data for newer agents, particularly faricimab and brolucizumab, are limited by shorter follow-up periods, and longer-term surveillance is required to characterize their risk profiles fully. Future directions Future research should prioritize long-term (>5-year) safety data, particularly for emerging agents such as faricimab. AI-driven predictive models could optimize dosing intervals by identifying responders to extended regimens. Biomarker studies are needed to elucidate mechanisms of treatment resistance in persistent DME. Additionally, cost-effectiveness analyses comparing biosimilars and novel agents in diverse healthcare systems would guide resource allocation. Conclusions This meta-analysis reaffirms aflibercept as first-line for severe DME, while faricimab offers a promising alternative with extended dosing. Bevacizumab biosimilars provide cost-effective options, albeit with higher injection frequency. Safety concerns with brolucizumab warrant cautious use. The substantial heterogeneity underscores the need for personalized treatment strategies based on baseline severity and dosing preferences. These findings support current clinical guidelines while highlighting gaps for future research. However, the extreme statistical heterogeneity across analyses (I² > 95%) weakens quantitative comparisons. It underscores the need to guide treatment decisions based on individual patient characteristics, including baseline VA, CRT, glycemic control, and treatment adherence, rather than relying solely on pooled effect estimates. Given the statistical complexity and residual unexplained variance, these findings would benefit from confirmation through individual patient data meta-analyses when such data become available.

documents.title: EURETINA guidelines for management of neovascular age-related macular degeneration

chunks.content: 1. Introduction Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is the leading cause of irreversible blindness in individuals over 65 years old and remains a major contributor to global visual impairment [ ]. The disease arises from a multifactorial etiology in which aging, cigarette smoking [ ], alcohol consumption [ ], hypertension [ ], diabetes, cardiovascular dysfunction, and chronic oxidative stress [ ] interact to accelerate retinal degeneration. These systemic risk factors converge on key pathological events, including progressive dysfunction of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), structural alterations in Bruch’s membrane, accumulation of drusen deposits [ ], and dysregulation of complement activation [ ]. The pathogenesis of AMD is a multifactorial process primarily initiated by chronic oxidative stress, which stems from the retina’s exceptionally high oxygen consumption and continuous exposure to photo-oxidative insults [ ]. This persistent stress leads to the progressive dysfunction of the RPE and the subsequent accumulation of lipofuscin, a result of impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments [ ]. These metabolic by-products contribute to the formation of drusen—extracellular deposits situated between the RPE and Bruch’s membrane—that act as a physical barrier hindering essential nutrient transport and metabolic waste removal. Such structural and biochemical alterations foster a state of chronic para-inflammation and significant dysregulation of the complement system, specifically involving the overactivation of C3 and C5 pathways [ , ]. Eventually, chronic oxidative mitochondrial damage and local hypoxia trigger the pathological upregulation of VEGF, driving the aberrant choroidal neovascularization (CNV) and vascular leakage characteristic of advanced exudative disease [ ]. Clinically, AMD encompasses a continuum from early stages to advanced forms, which the Beckman Initiative for Macular Research outlines through a five-stage classification system [ ]. In its late stages, AMD manifests as either atrophic (dry) or neovascular (wet) disease, with the neovascular subtype characterized by CNV, hemorrhage, and RPE detachment—events that account for severe vision loss in nearly 80% of affected patients [ , ]. As of current 2026 estimates based on recent epidemiological data, approximately 200 million individuals worldwide are living with some form of AMD [ ]. While the global burden is projected to reach nearly 288 million by 2040, this escalation is most pronounced in Asia [ , ]. By 2040, Asia is expected to account for approximately 113 million cases, representing the largest regional share of the global prevalence [ ]. In the Republic of Korea, a 2024 nationwide population-based study by the SNUBH research team revealed that the prevalence of exudative AMD has increased substantially over the last decade, with projections indicating a continued sharp rise as the nation becomes a super-aging society [ ]. Similarly, East Asian populations exhibit a distinct clinical profile; the Asia-Pacific PCV (polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy) Consensus Group has reported that PCV accounts for 22.3% to 54.7% of neovascular AMD cases in Asians, which is significantly higher than the 8% to 13% prevalence observed in Western cohorts [ ]. Critically, this escalating global burden highlights a significant nutritional gap, as current standard-of-care pharmacotherapies primarily target late-stage neovascular complications while leaving the underlying oxidative stress in early-to-intermediate AMD largely unaddressed. This underscores the urgent need for innovative dietary and delivery strategies—such as food-grade microgels—capable of mitigating retinal oxidative stress and inflammatory damage [ , ]. A central biological framework supporting the oral delivery of these bioactives is the gut–eye axis, a complex communication network that links intestinal homeostasis to retinal health [ ]. Emerging evidence suggests that gut dysbiosis and increased intestinal permeability can exacerbate retinal inflammation and CNV through the systemic translocation of pro-inflammatory cytokines and microbial metabolites [ ]. As illustrated in , the gut–eye axis functions as a systemic pathway where the modulation of the intestinal environment directly influences the blood–retinal barrier’s integrity and oxidative stress levels in the macula [ ]. By leveraging food-grade microgels to protect and target the delivery of nutrients within the gastrointestinal tract, it is possible to harness this axis to mitigate chronic retinal damage. Positioning the gut as a strategic gateway for retinal therapy provides a novel paradigm for AMD management, shifting the focus from local ocular treatments to systemic, diet-based interventions. Current clinical management of AMD primarily relies on photodynamic therapy (PDT), laser photocoagulation, and anti-VEGF–based pharmacotherapy [ ]. PDT employs intravenous administration of the photosensitizer verteporfin, which preferentially accumulates in abnormal sub-foveal vasculature. Nutrients for Alleviation of AMD Nutritional intervention has gained growing scientific attention as a complementary strategy for delaying the onset and progression of AMD, primarily because it addresses upstream biological mechanisms that precede irreversible photoreceptor loss. Oxidative stress, chronic para-inflammation, impaired mitochondrial turnover, and RPE dysfunction are now recognized as central nodes in AMD pathogenesis [ ]. Antioxidant vitamins—including vitamins C, E, and A derivatives—support retinal protection by neutralizing reactive oxygen species and maintaining photoreceptor viability, effects that were firmly established in the AREDS trial [ ]. However, subsequent analyses have shown that the efficacy of antioxidant therapy depends strongly on nutrient bioavailability and baseline dietary intake, with AREDS2 demonstrating that carotenoid-based formulations (lutein/zeaxanthin) outperform β-carotene in safety and biological relevance [ ]. Carotenoids such as lutein, zeaxanthin, and meso-zeaxanthin accumulate selectively in the macula through interactions with specific transport proteins, including scavenger receptor class B type 1 (SCARB1) and the lipid-transfer protein StARD3. Their functions extend beyond blue-light filtering to include quenching of singlet oxygen, stabilization of membrane lipids, and attenuation of photooxidative damage—mechanisms central to maintaining macular pigment optical density (MPOD), a strong biomarker of AMD risk. Similarly, long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (DHA/EPA) contribute to retinal health through anti-inflammatory lipid mediator synthesis (resolvins, protectins), enhancement of membrane fluidity, and support for photoreceptor outer segment renewal [ ]. Additional bioactives such as resveratrol, anthocyanins, curcumin, and zinc exhibit RPE-protective effects by modulating NF-κB signaling, complement activation, and mitochondrial redox homeostasis [ ]. Despite their mechanistic importance, many of these nutrients suffer from low water solubility, extensive first-pass metabolism, and poor gastrointestinal (GI) stability. Lipophilic nutrients like carotenoids and omega-3 fatty acids rely on bile-mediated emulsification and mixed micelle formation for absorption, processes that are highly inefficient when nutrients are delivered in crystalline or aggregated forms [ ]. Polyphenols undergo rapid oxidation or conjugation in the GI tract, limiting their systemic availability. These barriers highlight the need for delivery systems that improve solubilization, reduce oxidative degradation, and enhance trans-epithelial transport [ ]. Food-grade microgels offer a compelling solution to these challenges by integrating structural protection with physiologically compatible release mechanisms. The hydrated polymer networks of alginate-, pectin-, or protein-based microgels physically isolate labile nutrients from pro-oxidant environments, suppress isomerization of carotenoids, and stabilize omega-3 fatty acids against lipid peroxidation. Microgels can also modulate gastrointestinal transit behavior: their tunable mesh size and interfacial architecture promote improved lipid-phase dispersion, enhance bile salt accessibility, and facilitate uniform mixed micelle formation—key determinants of intestinal absorption [ ]. Importantly, the controlled swelling and enzymatic responsiveness of microgels allow nutrient release to align with peak absorption in the duodenum and jejunum, providing a level of spatiotemporal control not achievable through conventional supplementation. The coupling of established nutrient-based interventions with microgel-enabled delivery systems may substantially enhance their biological efficacy, offering a next-generation approach for nutritional modulation of AMD progression. Physicochemical Approaches Physicochemical methods generate microgels by inducing molecular association, conformational transitions, or electrostatic interactions within or between biopolymers. These methods often operate under mild processing conditions, which is advantageous for protecting antioxidants and carotenoids vulnerable to thermal or oxidative degradation [ , ]. Although each physicochemical route differs in its underlying mechanism, all share the capacity to produce microgels with tunable porosity, hydration, and barrier properties. Self-association is one of the most versatile routes for microgel formation because it leverages the natural responsiveness of biopolymers. For globular proteins such as whey protein isolate (WPI), β-lactoglobulin, or ovalbumin, heating above their denaturation temperatures unfolds tertiary structures and exposes hydrophobic residues and thiol groups. These domains aggregate through hydrophobic interactions and disulfide bonding to form colloidal protein microgels with particle sizes ranging from tens of nanometers to several micrometers, depending on pH, protein concentration, and ionic strength [ , ]. Importantly, these hydrophobic pockets and amphiphilic surfaces provide a favorable microenvironment for entrapping highly lipophilic AMD-related compounds such as lutein and zeaxanthin, thereby preventing oxidative degradation during storage and digestion. Cold-set gelation provides a complementary alternative for heat-sensitive bioactives. In this process, proteins are first thermally denatured under controlled conditions and then rapidly cooled. Subsequent crosslinking—often induced by Ca 2+ —results in microgels with softer textures and narrower size distributions [ , ]. These cold-set microgels maintain high encapsulation efficiencies while avoiding additional thermal stress, making them particularly suitable for carotenoids and antioxidant polyphenols. Polysaccharides, including alginate, pectin, and gellan gum, undergo self-assembly primarily through ionic crosslinking. For instance, alginate forms “egg-box” junction zones with Ca 2+ , producing hydrogel networks with excellent biocompatibility and structural stability [ ]. These networks exhibit strong barrier properties against oxygen and light exposure—both major causes of carotenoid degradation—highlighting their suitability for encapsulating sensitive AMD-related bioactives. Associative complexation, frequently manifested as complex coacervation, results from electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged polymers. Examples include systems such as whey protein–pectin, gelatin–gum arabic, or casein–alginate. Encapsulation of Probiotics Probiotic microorganisms are among the most demanding cargos for any ingestible delivery system: they must remain viable during processing and storage, resist acid and bile exposure in the stomach and duodenum, and then colonize the distal gut to exert metabolic, immunomodulatory, or barrier-repair functions [ , ]. Food-grade microgel systems for probiotics respond to these constraints using polysaccharide- and protein-based matrices that act as physical shelters (“silkworm cocoons”), typically surrounding the bacterial cells with one or more protective layers, or as networked gel environments (“spider webs”), in which the bacteria are embedded in a hydrated 3D mesh that limits diffusive access of acid, oxidants, and bile salts. A common strategy is the formation of ionically crosslinked alginate microgels, often further coated with secondary biopolymers such as chitosan or pectin to build multilayer shells with pH-responsive behavior [ ]. Recent in vitro studies (2024–2025) have quantified the efficacy of these architectures, demonstrating that multilayered beads can maintain probiotic viability above 85% after 2 h of exposure to simulated gastric fluid (pH 2.0), whereas non-encapsulated cells show near-total depletion [ , ]. These multilayered coatings reduce proton and bile penetration in simulated gastric fluid, thereby preserving cell viability, and subsequently swell or partially disassemble at near-neutral intestinal pH to permit controlled release and colonization in the lower gut. Inclusion of buffering microdomains (for example, carbonate phases) or lipid droplets within the same microgel can further suppress local acidification and slow the ingress of harmful species, which improves survival through the stomach while deferring release until later intestinal segments where colonization is beneficial. In addition to pH protection, surface charge engineering of the outer shell can be exploited to enhance mucosal adhesion. For example, cationic or thiolated polysaccharide coatings can interact electrostatically or via disulfide exchange with negatively charged colonic mucins, which prolongs residence time in inflamed or dysbiotic regions and supports more localized therapeutic action [ ]. Taken together, these encapsulation strategies translate pharmaceutical principles of protection, site-specific delivery, and mucosal localization into fully food-grade probiotic formats, potentially modulating the gut–retina axis for AMD management. 5.2.
